Title: my THIRD mit science bowl [liveblog]
Author: Suzuko O. '30
Article Content: …but now i’m on the other side November 13, 2026 when i was in high school, the thing that took up the most amount of my time was science bowl.⁠01science bowl is a government-sponsored competition where you win if you push buttons faster and answer questions more correctly than the other team does. want to see how it works? go watch last year’s mit scibowl finals video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uW-jb2qBkXofor hours upon hours every week i would find myself sitting in mr maine’s well-ornamented room after school (tuesdays and thursdays, until 6!), or back hunched leaning over my computer, thumb poised over my space-bar like a trigger, or closing my eyes and waiting for sleep as the seeds of questions and the skeletons of tournament brackets raced through my head. picture of a nats competition stage! my junior year mit scibowl was the first time that i remember coming to mit. it was a magical time – on friday night, we got dinner with alumni at saloniki’s; afterwards, steph and boheng, then freshmen in college (now juniors!), led me and my team and my friends on a wild-goose chase through the tunnels of mit. on saturday we played the tournament; after dinner with friends, we watched mit spinning arts club’s novemburn show and then my team stayed up playing party games until 4am. in senior year, remembering all the fun i had the year before, i counted down the days until comp – until i could visit alumni, until i could play against disembodied friends from across the country, until i could hug people i hadn’t seen since summer. there were probably more but i gave up on finding them it’s not an exaggeration to say that science bowl is the main reason that i’m here at mit now. science bowl gave me the community and the enrichment and the challenge that i craved in high school; it gave me a reason to drag myself through the drudgery of a school day to make it to practice and dopamine and friends. with everything scibowl gave me, i was certain i wanted to give back. mit scibowl runs on an annual cycle: question writing begins and is completed in the summer; editing starts with the school year, slowly transitioning into logistics; the tournament itself runs in mid-november, just as the air chills and starts to bite. this summer i wrote questions for biology, earth science, and energy, showing up to weekly playtesting meetings.⁠02when i could - sometimes travel got in the way school started and i started showing up to mit exec meetings. more question-editing, some logistics – me and some other frosh brainstormed mit scibowl’s first set of friday night activities, for students the night before the competition. yet even as i committed weekly time to scibowl, i eventually realized that somehow – without me really noticing its happening – it had slipped my mind, like a skate on ice. no longer did science bowl occupy dozens of hours of my brainspace a week. yet i’ve still been counting down the days till this mit science bowl! now my excitement is driven not by my desire to play (because of course my role is no longer to play). now i want to put on a good show, help our tournament directors make sure everything runs smoothly. and honestly the biggest part is that my brother !!! and my mom !!! and friends !!! are coming !!! to visit :) this year’s mit science bowl will be the largest ever. we’re inviting 60 teams of 5 players each to campus, relying on a team of over a hundred volunteers, games stretching from a crisp 9am⁠03volunteers need to be ready by 8 - i don't know when the last time i woke up before 8am was to 8pm if necessary. this year, i won’t be in the game rooms themselves;⁠04or at least i’m not planned to be instead i’ll be running whatever administrative errands are necessary to help keep the tournament going smoothly. over the next 24 hours, i’ll be writing about this event i love so much – now from a different perspective. if you’re playing, good luck! i hope you have fun C: if not, stay along for the ride :) this year we’re introducing science PLATE, which stands for Pre-tournament exhiLArating Team Events. since a lot of teams (like my high school’s) travel to cambridge ahead of time, we wanted to have something chill for the kids to do on friday night. this year we’ve prepared scrimmages (where teams play each other in friendly matches for practice), some board games, some light food, some printed puzzles, and (my personal favorite) karaoke! right now we’ve just finished the opening ceremony, and the kids are playing a kahoot to get them somewhat oriented about how mit is laid out (so that they can find the rooms they need to play in tomorrow). do they know what room we’re currently in? (kinda) do they know what building the opening ceremony is in? (no) look at all those answers we’re in 4-163, which is like a lecture hall type room. the room is almost full with kids! most seats are taken. it’s nice to see that everyone is pulling up. side note – something that’s kinda fried is that all flights nationally are grounded right now. this is bad for teams that were going to take red-eyes to get here, as well as some volunteers, like the connors from my high school team. they are stuck in the bay area… i really hope that flights are sorted out soon but i doubt it will be. this is pretty evil ngl i suppose i should figure out some sort of karaoke layout? likely it is important for me to find the light switches and whatnot 7:35pm okay after some brief technical difficulties i got karaoke working like thirty minutes ago! sound wasn’t working and youtube wasn’t loading on the shared screen, but it turns out restarting your computer fixes a lot of problems. my theory of karaoke is that you need a critical mass of people singing before new people feel comfortable joining in. this is because all people are intrinsically awkward, and people who do science competitions in high school are especially so. luckily my awkward limbo was saved by the entire two teams of pioneer charter high who immediately lit up the room with their energy we went through a lot of songs but i don’t remember all of them – sunflower, hot to go, riptide, beauty and a beat. we still have like an hour and a half left so i’m hoping that the high level of sound being emitted from this room will summon more children (the more the merrier!) bonus points if you can guess the song! 9:44pm PLATE is now over! i had a good time; the room was never empty and there was continuous songs basically from like 7:10 to 9, when we ended. unfortunately for admin-side the work isn’t over for the night. usually we have lots of stuff set out ahead of time – brackets, room signs, etc – but the 3 hour flight stoppage has thrown a wrench into our plans. we have already had 3 teams that are guaranteed not able to make it all the way to boston because their flights got cancelled, and some of our volunteers (exemplified by my friends connor and connor) are stuck across the country, which means we need to shuffle volunteers around to make sure that all the rooms are staffed. i was initially planning to go to my friend’s room but i think there is too much to do to justify that hopefully i do not stay up super late because i really can’t function on little sleep :skull: 11:04pm okay i am in my bed now preparing to sleep. there are still a lot of admin in stud working on things for tomorrow – finding 6 more boxes and 11 more extension cords, etc. we put off bracketing stuff and room signs until tomorrow morning at 6:30am, meaning that i have to be awake in less than 7.5 hours… i think 6:30 is the earliest that i have been awake in maybe half a year? barring plane stuff or whatever, and this is the first time i’m sleeping before midnight in a while. i think as a competitor i really did not understand all the work that has to be done adminside. especially this year since we expanded our field by 25%, it is definitely a significant amount of extra stress (in the mechanical sense) that is not helping the structural integrity of our tournament but also i am pretty optimistic that everything will be alright. i guess one thing that i prided myself on in high school was my general competence – my ability to handle a lot of different things generally well – and here i haven’t really yet felt that yet. i’m not the person at the head of this tournament, of course, but i think mit science bowl is somewhere where i can do my best in whatever needs to be done and smooth the path for competitors good night and see you tomorrow morning! Title: Slinging π’s
Author: Nicholas R. '29
Article Content: thinking about my first time on MIT's campus November 10, 2026 The other day I was walking to Next House. I was by myself, headphones on, in the middle of a downpour—completely soaked yet steadfast in my journey to eat the best dining-hall chicken tenders and fries on campus.⁠01I love Next Dining. It's objectively the best MIT dining hall, which isn't a very high bar but still. I was hungry. Food was on my mind. On my way past the tennis courts I was seized by a string of memories. First, it was of pizza. Then, naturally, it was of when I first stepped foot on MIT’s campus, over four years ago… It’s freshly summer, and I’m a soon-to-be sophomore in high school. It’s my second summer working at a local pizza restaurant called Pizza Barbone. I started as a dishwasher, but this summer I’ve been promoted to pizza-maker. In addition to the restaurant itself, Barbone has mobile pizza-oven trucks and offers catering across Cape Cod and, occasionally, the Greater Boston area. I’m on my very first catering event, admittedly a bit nervous as I ride shotgun in the truck with my boss, Jason. After over an hour of driving, we’re just now entering the city; we make our way through the Boston traffic and are soon rolling down Memorial Drive, past Maseeh and other less castle-like dorms. We park the truck in front of a fraternity⁠02I think it was DKE or maybe KS and are greeted by our clients: a group of college-aged guys, presumably students in the frat. We begin setting up our workspace and preparing the pizzas. Given that I’m still early on in my pizza-making journey, Jason guides me through the process of stretching the dough and topping it. I feel the dough awkwardly sag and slip through my fingers—I didn’t yet have the proper technique⁠03Let the dough drape over your knuckles, slowly move your fists apart in a circular motion, and let gravity do most of the work! to prevent it from tearing or stretching too thin. After forming some questionably-shaped pies,⁠04Slang for pizzas I start topping while Jason feeds the glowing brick oven some wood chips. Once the fire is going, the pizzas get fed to the oven, and the dough rises and bubbles, forming a beautiful Neopolitan crust. I watch the freshly-cooked pizzas be carried inside the building, which has slowly been filling up with guests during our prep. I hear standard fare from a college-party playlist⁠05Quintessential frat songs like 'Clarity,' 'No Hands,' 'Doses & Mimosas,' etc. blasting through speakers, competing with the cheerful shouts and chatter from the people inside. In that moment I feel as if I’m staring at an exhibition: this is what college looks like, just as I have seen in the movies. I look behind me. There’s people walking by, one is repping an MIT hoodie. There’s some other figures on the court, playing tennis. The sun tries peeking through the overcast. That’s about where the memory ended, just as I was clouded with thoughts of chicken tenders and fries. I hadn’t thought about that moment in a long time. It’s strange and maybe poetic to think about how I was staring at my future, in a way. That was really the first time I remember thinking about college, or what I would do beyond high school, in a serious way. It still felt so far away. I still had at least a few more summers to work at Barbone, after all. And that restaurant job was very formative for me: I learned many cliché yet important things about myself and working with others in a professional setting. Four years later, I’m here and I still have much to learn. The more you see, the less you know. Anyways, I want to end this meandering blog with a small piece of unsolicited advice. To current or prospective applicants: don’t shy away from talking about high school jobs in your college applications. If it was formative to yourself as a person, then I’d argue it’s worthy of mentioning—whether it is particularly glamorous or not, academic or not. I remember feeling hesitant about including my “silly” summer job on my applications. I thought it might be better to include something that was academic-leaning, but I realized there was nothing that I could’ve replaced it with that felt as personally significant as slinging pies. Title: Something to believe in
Author: Janet G. '27
Article Content: and say goodbye to November 9, 2026 MIT is not known for its polish or ease. We are a cramped-up campus of noisy, scrappy, endless construction; we are college students who are too busy to look happy or well-groomed; we only really have two types of weather, too-hot-and-humid and too-dark-and-cold. But we work with what we have: we make affectionate nicknames out of our buildings and all their odd shapes and histories; we embrace the camaraderie that comes from drinking the firehose; we hold onto the brief weeks when the sun peeks through the clouds, with bright blue skies and golden foliage and the shimmering Charles, and remember the other meanings of IHTFP. We work with what we have, and we make something out of it. the shimmering charles Let me show you something from September 19th. Come with me as I jump out of bed at 10am on a Saturday morning when I would otherwise be asleep; follow me through the dewy grass and under the big white tent that seems to have sprouted up on Kresge lawn overnight, and collect an engraved navy badge and an illustrated tote bag from some beaming sleep-deprived organisers in bright yellow hoodies; talk to the students lugging suitcases and neck pillows next to you and learn that they flew over from Berkeley or Illinois or Switzerland to attend this hackathon; join a thousand people in Kresge Auditorium to listen to 3Blue1Brown give his first in-person talk at MIT since COVID; follow the crowd outside past the laser-cut and heat-pressed wonderland-themed flags adorning the lightpoles; walk down the brick path and into the Z Center, ⁠01what we call our main athletics complex and look at how the grey and silver walls are now plastered with pastel streamers, shiny balloons, and jumbo-sized handmade playing cards; pick up a macaron from the snack stand and then put it down upon realising it’s just really well-made clay; go into the Johnson Ice Rink, the thing you might know as a grey, cold, concrete, hollow beast, and realise that it’s suddenly been taken over by rows and rows of pastel tables and pink lights and balloon arches and great big projector screens, and you could call it beautiful. September 19th was the first day of my last HackMIT, the first one that I’ve attended and not organised. This blog is about HackMIT, the club I spent three years organising and directing. It is also about my life, the institutions I’ve been involved in, and how we’ve shaped each other. I’ve been working on this blog for a year now. There’s always more I could improve on, more days I could spend writing, rewriting, revising it. But I’ve sunk enough time into it, and I need to move on. So even when there’s more to do, even when something is precious to you, we work with what we have, and sometimes we have to let things go. To understand how HackMIT mattered to me, you first need to understand who I am. I spent the first 18 years of my life living in Hamilton, New Zealand. Hamilton is the fourth-largest city in New Zealand, but most people stop caring after the top three.⁠02Auckland is the largest city and is what most people usually know; Christchurch is the largest city in the South Island and you might also know it from the shooting a few years ago; Wellington is our capital All the schools I went to were decile 5, certified average by the New Zealand education system. I never did out-of-school extracurriculars and spent most of my childhood rolling around in dirt, surfing youtube, and reading webnovels. I was the only second grader at my school asked to take a talent aptitude test, but they never followed up; I was nominated for Sports Girl of the Year at school because I won cross country, but only because the fastest girl fell over in the middle of the race; I lucked my way into the top three of my regional spelling bee, but proceeded to be the first person to get eliminated at the national bee. ⁠03it was a five-letter word from a list of words i was supposed to have memorised… latke… you never forget the word that gets you your fated ding A stereotype is that MIT students are all labelled as exceptional from a young age: gifted, talented, prodigy. I was none of these things; I was an average kid who was smart enough, but only in my decile 5 school in the fourth-largest city in a small island country people don’t even remember to include on maps. The only label I could describe myself with was hungry. I was hungry to prove myself, and I jumped at every chance I had for a competition, which was not often when you’re from Hamilton. I never seemed to be the best, but I was relentless: I got a 0 on the maths olympiad entrance exam and came back for three more years; I spilled half the sample over my biology exam paper and finished my writeup on the soggy pages anyway; I was told by my junior debate teacher that I needed to “accept that [I] won’t always get a chance to speak when [better debater] needs the training opportunity more,” so I watched practice speeches on my own every day. I never won anything—always honourable mention, top 40, second place—but I never stopped trying. Honourable mentions can make it into the maths olympiad national camp, top 40s can win IBO⁠04the international biology olympiad silver medals, second places can captain the national debate team. Maybe I’m just a typical⁠05#forgotten #feelingoverlookedmiddle child. My parents were always comfortable with my mediocre successes, since it allowed them to squabble and fuss over other things—my siblings, their jobs, each other. They reacted to all the achievements I brought home in the same way: a pleasantly surprised acknowledgement that lasted between ten and fifteen seconds. They had a stronger reaction when I told them that I wanted to apply to American colleges: “Why would you want to do that? America is far. Also, you’re probably not going to get in anyway.” They weren’t wrong. I was an aid-needing international student applying to top schools. So I leaned into the labels that would make me admissible: biology olympian, debater, theatre nerd, quirky kiwi. Fitting your life into a thousand words of application materials can feel like training to be a contortionist, but it was necessary to stand out as an applicant in a sea of thirty thousand. When I got into MIT, I called my parents about it. The first thing my mum said was, “How much does it cost? Why can’t you just do medicine at the University of Auckland?⁠06Since the New Zealand school year ends in December, I was already enrolled at an NZ university while I was waiting for my college results. This is common practice for southern hemisphere universities, and also meant that I needed to persuade my parents to let me leave my NZ university. You’d be a pretty decent doctor.” But I saw a new identity tied to an institution that I’d barely dared to dream about. It would open doors, give me the resources and community to accomplish feats I couldn’t even imagine, and free me from needing to settle for the option my parents thought safest. I was going to prove my parents wrong: I wasn’t going to be a decent doctor comfortable with mediocre successes. After heated arguments, angry tears, and a generous financial aid offer, I was ready to call myself an MIT student. My initial vision of an MIT student may have been overambitious: they were geniuses but also studious; they were firehose drinkers but also effortlessly organised; they were party animals but also led five clubs at once. I thought it was doable; after all, I got into MIT. It couldn’t be that hard, right? But MIT humbles everyone, whether you like it or not. I failed a 6.100A⁠07our intro to CS course quiz in my first semester and pulled a bunch of all-nighters over 8.01⁠08our intro physics course, mechanics. i HATED that class psets. I tried out 6-7 clubs and still dropped basically all of them. I hated debating in the APDA format,⁠09american parliamentary debate format; i debated in the world schools format in high school I got too afraid of the Shakespeare memorisation commitment, I wasn’t inspired to write poetry anymore, and I couldn’t afford to budget the number of hours required to enjoy Acapella and Mock Trial. HackMIT was going to be just another club on the list. I forgot to apply to participate during the summer. I went to the organiser application info session only because friends said there was free boba. I also forgot about the organiser deadline, and only remembered when I saw a friend applying in the flounge at 10pm. I debated whether the long application was worth my effort, then wrote the app in 30 minutes and submitted at 11:50pm. I almost missed my interview the next day, and while I was excited in my response to the acceptance email, I was still thinking about the other applications I needed to fill out while I waited with the other new members to enter the welcome meeting. Everything changed the moment I walked into the room. We were surrounded by cheering from Lili, Albert, ⁠10the co-directors of HackMIT 2023 and the rest of the team, and they kept the energy throughout the entire evening: we went through a million introductions with everyone’s names and class titles, a huge spreadsheet with comic sans and fluorescent colours and signup slots going from 6am to 9pm, an endless list of tasks, a countdown of five days until my first HackMIT, a vision of the chaos to come, and somehow all of it was getting transcribed by Albert at 200 wpm. It was then that I decided this community was for me, and I would do everything I could to become embedded in it. But wait—what does HackMIT even do? HackMIT is a student club at MIT which runs two hackathons a year.⁠11Hackathons are focused events in which people get a constrained window of time to prototype and demo a project in its entirety.HackMIT is also the name of our flagship collegiate hackathon hosted in the fall, while Blueprint is a hackathon for 300 high schoolers hosted in the spring. To disambiguate between the club and the hackathon, we will from now on call the club Hack. To run the events, we have a very structured form of leadership: team members are led by committee heads, who are led by one director during the Blueprint-planning cycle, and two directors during the HackMIT-planning cycle. We start the school year with HackMIT, which is led by two co-directors. After HackMIT, the senior co-director retires, and the new solo director runs Blueprint, our high school hackathon. The team plans through fall and winter to run Blueprint in the spring, and director elections happen after Blueprint to elect a new junior co-director. The two co-directors then lead the team through spring and summer to plan out HackMIT in the fall, the now-senior co-director retires, and the cycle repeats. Blueprint 2024: learning the ropes Onboarding at my first welcome meeting was chaotic, but that’s just how Hack is: it skews younger as a club,⁠12in any given year, Hack is around 40-50% freshmen, 30-40% sophomores, and 10-20% upperclassmen so it trusts and expects new recruits to pick things up and run with them, whether you’ve had the relevant experience or not. This also informs the leadership structure: you can apply to be a committee head right after you join, and you can be trusted enough to be selected. I was one such case: I ran for head of corporate relations right after HackMIT 2023, five weeks into freshman fall. I had to learn to scope out project timelines and coordinate with other committees, run weekly meetings and encourage team members when they were unmotivated, and balance our efforts between student outreach and corporate sponsorships. It was challenging. But in the end, I was proud of how Blueprint 2024 turned out. It was now time for the next cycle of elections, and I had a lot of thinking to do. Freshman year I struggled a lot in freshman year. Some of the issues were about Hack, some of them were about moving ten thousand kilometres away from home and learning to live by myself, some of them were about being an MIT student. Everyone else seemed to be a great MIT student: taking more advanced classes while still doing well in them, landing internship offers at [Big Tech firms], doing meaningful research through UROPs. So when I was thinking about running for director in the spring, I was also asking myself: What have I done with my life? I’d dropped all but two of my clubs. I could barely get through a pset without asking for help from friends. I hated the career fairs and had nothing to tell the companies. I found a research opportunity for the summer, but didn’t have much relevant experience and wondered if I would get anything out of it. It felt like all I was doing was struggling in my classes, feeling unhirable, and organising for Hack. So in a way, Hack director was a label I felt that I needed: it was compensation for everything else that I hadn’t done. I wasn’t being a studious researcher, a technical intern, or an academic weapon. I was just a jobless quirky kiwi who did stuff with Hack. I told my parents that I would show them just how much more I could do as an MIT student. What was I going to tell them now? Director elections I really wanted to become a director. I loved the club, and I had Opinions that I wanted to enact, but a big motivator was the insecurities I built up in freshman year, and I’m not going to deny that I felt competitive about it. After all, I spent years grinding for all-or-nothing competitions. But as I talked to the older directors and thought about why I wanted to run, I learned to embrace a different perspective: being a director is not just a title for your resume and ego, but a serious commitment that you will have to make sacrifices for. It is a role that you will grow a lot in, and you will be contributing to a community that you love, but the directorship isn’t the only role in Hack which provides that kind of fulfilment: committee heads also get a lot of leadership experience, and committed team members can also heavily shape the direction of Hack and get credit and growth for important projects. There are trade-offs to everything. Two of my closest friends from Hack, Maggie and Alison, also ran for director. We doodled on the chalkboard, jumped up and down together to shake off our nerves, and coordinated “theme songs” that we would play when we entered to speak with the team. I was still nervous, but I knew that I could contribute to Hack as either a committee head or director, and I would get to work with Maggie and Alison, so these elections were going to turn out great regardless of the results. The point of director elections is to show the team a vision of what Hack will look like under your leadership, and to trust in their decision for the future they’re most excited about. When I was announced as the newest director, Maggie and Alison swarmed me in a group hug, and we were once again jumping up and down together. They became some of the best committee heads who I’ve worked with, and are still some of my closest friends to this day. After elections, I wrote in my notes app: 1. i am now director and that means that i have the weight of a team on my back. i have to be stronger with more personal resolve so that i can actually survive under all my responsibilities. 2. the people who run for hack director are also super passionate and i’m so excited for hack cycle heads and yayyyy Becoming director was the biggest responsibility of my life; there was no turning back now. I couldn’t wait for the next 1.5 years. I told myself I’d do everything: I was going to lead the community, scale up the hackathon, and do whatever it would take to be the best Hack director possible. HackMIT 2024: how to be a director An institution is a relatively stable collection of rules and practices, embedded in structures of resources that make action possible – organisational, financial and staff capabilities, and structures of meaning that explain and justify behaviour – roles, identities and belongings, common purposes, and causal and normative beliefs. (March and Olsen, 1989, original emphasis) — Why Institutions Matter, Vivian Lowndes and Mark Roberts I joined as the 13th director to lead Hack. There had been over a decade of knowledge, mistakes, and adaptations built up before I arrived, and I spent the first few weeks as director absorbing as much knowledge as I could. At the time, this all felt like a slog through long conversations and notes app logs and Google Docs dating back years, but now I can formalise it: there were rules, practices, and narratives I had to learn, because these were the ways in which institutions (Hack) do their work (run a hackathon). As the co-directors of Hack, Albert and I jumped into 6+ hours of meetings each week, for the committees, the team-wide generals, and syncs between us and committee heads. We started negotiating with MIT admin for various different things that we needed from them: overnight venue access, sponsorship packet approvals, so on and so forth. We pored over previous iterations of meeting notes to determine how we wanted to structure our general meetings, figuring out the messaging that we wanted the entire team to buy into: why do we spend so much time working on a hackathon? What does it mean for a hackathon to be good for the hackers? How do we want people to remember this hackathon? Aside from all the director-specific problems, I learned much more about all the different committees in Hack. Every committee had distinct problems at scales that I’d never quite encountered before. We designed a new architecture to merge our major devops platforms, we experimented with new ways to make the theme more design-focused rather than illustration-focused, we negotiated with startups and tech firms to acquire hundreds of thousands of dollars, and we negotiated with MIT admin and restaurants and merch vendors to spend it. I had the resources to solve these problems, and I understood why people found power to be addicting. I could make things happen and it was awesome. I leaned in, and let the title of Hack director consume my life. I quit ESP,⁠13Education Studies Program, a really lovely club that runs education events for mostly middle and high schoolers! the only other club I was in, stopped applying to jobs since I’d found my summer UROP, and spent all day outside of classes thinking about how to do more with Hack. Every bit of work I put in was reflected in our progress towards HackMIT 2024. It wasn’t all sunshine and rainbows. I felt guilty about dropping the ball for ESP multiple times. There were days when I got back home after a day of class or a day in the lab, and had to resist the urge to rot in bed in order to sit through 3+ hours of meetings or battle a spreadsheet. I learned to manage my own emotions, to organise my time, and to communicate firmly but kindly to people when they slacked off. Hack was the reason I got out of bed, my doomscrolling mechanism, and the catalyst behind most of the ways in which I grew. how to say goodbye, part one HackMIT 2024 came and went. The play-by-play is in the old blog that I wrote. What I remember from it now is the pride that swelled in me as I stepped onto the Kresge stage; the chaos of running around during judging; rolling around in the moving carts as we wound down after a long day. I remember sitting with Albert and Emily ⁠14the Blueprint 2023 and HackMIT 2023 logistics head, and one of my favourite people ever <3 she made me feel super welcome in hack and was one of the big reasons why I loved hack so much in MacGregor after the hackathon ended, ordering burgers and fries from Tasty Burger and eating them with dining hall ketchup packets we saved, laughing about not being on the same wavelengths, thinking about how this was now the end of an era. It might be an understatement to say that I was devastated when Albert left. He defined Hack as I had known it. I relied on him for advice both inside and outside of Hack, and we were two peas in a pod: sitting together in every meeting, always a topic to discuss, always a new joke to tell. Being a director was hard, but I knew that I could always rely on him when I didn’t want to run a meeting, or when I didn’t know how to have a difficult conversation, or when I just didn’t know how to do a certain task. Now that HackMIT was over, I had to run Blueprint by myself, and I had big shoes to fill. Blueprint 2025: how to take on independence Most major hackathon organisers only organise one hackathon a year: the amount of time required to invest in a thousand-person hackathon on top of school, work, and life is already a huge commitment. Still, we organise two hackathons and constrain ourselves to ~7 months for HackMIT. How does this high school hackathon justify the cost of needing to work all year round while compressing organising timelines for our flagship hackathon? It’s because Blueprint is awesome. We teach high school students CS and hardware and make things for the sake of it, and we get to support educational access and give back to the local community.
